newsitem.title: FRANCE: Employees protest closure of France's Superphenix.
newsitem.headline: Employees protest closure of France's Superphenix.

text.p: Nearly 2,000 people protested in eastern France on Monday against plans by the new Left-wing government to close the controversial Superphenix fast-breeder nuclear reactor.

Members of the Communist-led CGT union and employees of state-owned utility Electricite de France (EDF), the reactor's majority owner, staged the demonstration outside the problem-plagued plant in the Alpine town of Creys-Malville to protest what they say would lead to the loss of 5,000 jobs.
They also warned of the high cost of an early closure for EDF and the dire loss of tax revenues for the region.
New Environment Minister Dominique Voynet, leader of the Greens party, wants to scrap the plant, which has been the bete noire of environmentalists since it was built 20 years ago.
Before the Left swept to power in June 1 elections, Voynet denounced the 60 billion franc ($10.5 billion) plant as a waste of money and vowed to shut it down.
The demonstrators said the closure would force 700 EDF employees out of their jobs, while another 3,500 jobs would be lost in other firms linked to the reactor.
A disputed 1995 government study said it would cost up to 20 billion francs ($3 billion) to close the plant two decades ahead of the scheduled date of 2020.
But opponents counter that the plant costs 600 million francs ($103 million) a year to keep in operation.
The 1,200-megawatt reactor's future may become clearer on Thursday when Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin outlines his plans in his first policy statement to the National Assembly.
Superphenix, which is 51 percent-owned by EDF with Italy's ENEL and a Dutch-German-Belgian consortium as partners, was built to produce more plutonium than it consumed.
But dogged by constant problems, it has been on line for only 30 months and fed the electricity grid for only 10 months.
The government downgraded it in 1994, allowing it to operate at reduced power only as a research tool into nuclear waste disposal.
